entries.46:8: This begins a list of the names of Jacob's family who came to Egypt, starting with Reuben, his firstborn. It shows that God cares about ordinary people by name, and the reader can know they matter to him too.
entries.46:9: These were Reuben's four sons: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. It's a family record showing the promise to Abraham was growing through real, named people.
entries.46:10: These were Simeon's sons, including Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite woman. It shows the family was mixed and imperfect, yet still part of God's plan.
entries.46:11: These were Levi's three sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. It's a simple record of a family line that later became important in Israel's worship.
entries.46:12: These were Judah's sons; two of them, Er and Onan, had already died in Canaan, and Perez had two sons. It shows that even with loss and tragedy in a family, God's plan keeps moving forward.
entries.46:13: These were Issachar's four sons: Tola, Puah, Job, and Shimron. It's another family record showing the growing number of Jacob's descendants.
entries.46:14: These were Zebulun's three sons: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. It's a brief record reminding the reader that each tribe and family had real, named beginnings.
entries.46:15: This lists Leah's children and Dinah, thirty-three in all, born to Jacob in Paddan-aram. It shows how one branch of the family grew large, fulfilling God's promise of many descendants.
entries.46:16: These were Gad's seven sons: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. It's a family record showing the promise continuing through each son.
entries.46:17: These were Asher's children, including his sister Sarah, and his grandsons through Beriah. It shows that both sons and daughters were counted in the family of God's people.
entries.46:18: This lists the sixteen children Jacob had through Zilpah, the servant Laban gave to Leah. It shows that even the less prominent members of the family were part of God's promise.
entries.46:19: These were the sons of Jacob's wife Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. It highlights the line that mattered most to the story, since Joseph was already in Egypt.
entries.46:20: Joseph had two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, in Egypt with Asenath, the daughter of a priest of On. It shows God blessed Joseph even in a foreign land.
entries.46:21: These were Benjamin's ten sons. It shows the youngest brother's family was already large, a sign of God's blessing on the whole family.
entries.46:22: This counts Rachel's descendants through Jacob as fourteen people. It's a simple tally showing the promise growing through Rachel's line.
entries.46:23: Dan had one son, Hushim. It's a short record reminding the reader that even small families were part of the whole.
entries.46:24: These were Naphtali's four sons: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. It's another brief family record in the larger list.
entries.46:25: This lists the seven children Jacob had through Bilhah, the servant Laban gave to Rachel. It shows the family's full size and that God's promise included every branch.
entries.46:26: Counting only Jacob's direct descendants who came to Egypt, not the wives of his sons, there were sixty-six. It shows the family had grown large, just as God had promised.
entries.46:27: Joseph had two sons in Egypt, bringing the total of Jacob's family in Egypt to seventy. It shows God's promise of many descendants was coming true.
entries.46:28: Jacob sent Judah ahead to Goshen to get directions from Joseph, and then they arrived there. It shows careful planning and the family settling where Joseph intended.
entries.46:29: Joseph rode in his chariot to meet his father in Goshen and hugged him, weeping. It's a picture of deep family love and forgiveness after years apart.
entries.46:30: Jacob told Joseph that now that he had seen him alive, he could die in peace. It shows how much this reunion meant to him, and how God had answered his grief.
entries.46:31: Joseph told his brothers and father's household that he would go tell Pharaoh that his family had come from Canaan. It shows Joseph preparing to represent his family honestly before the king.
entries.46:32: Joseph explained that his family were shepherds and cattle owners with their flocks and herds and everything they had. It shows he was setting up an honest account of who they were.
entries.46:33: Joseph told them that when Pharaoh asks what their work is, they should be ready to answer. It's practical advice to be honest and prepared when questioned by authority.
entries.46:34: Joseph told them to say they had been cattle keepers all their lives, like their fathers, so they could settle in Goshen, since Egyptians looked down on shepherds. It shows God using even a cultural prejudice to give his people a place to live.
entries.47:1: Joseph told Pharaoh that his father and brothers had arrived from Canaan with all their animals and belongings, and were now settled in Goshen. This shows Joseph being honest with the king about his family's arrival.
entries.47:2: Joseph brought five of his brothers to meet Pharaoh personally. He wanted the king to know his family directly, not just hear about them.
entries.47:3: Pharaoh asked the brothers what work they did, and they answered that they were shepherds, just like their ancestors. They were being straightforward about their trade.
entries.47:4: The brothers explained they had come because there was no grass for their animals in Canaan, and they asked permission to stay in Goshen. They were asking politely for a place to live and work.
entries.47:5: Pharaoh told Joseph to let his family settle in Goshen, and to put any capable men in charge of his own livestock. The king trusted Joseph's family with real responsibility.
entries.47:6: When Pharaoh heard Joseph's family had arrived, he told Joseph to give them the best land in Egypt to live in. The king showed generosity because of his respect for Joseph.
entries.47:7: Joseph brought his father Jacob to meet Pharaoh, and Jacob greeted him with a blessing. Even as a foreign refugee, Jacob offered the king a gesture of goodwill.
entries.47:8: Pharaoh asked Jacob how old he was. It was a simple, friendly question to get to know the old man.
entries.47:9: Jacob said he had lived 130 years, but described them as few and hard compared to his ancestors' long lives. He was honest that his life had been full of struggle.
entries.47:10: Jacob blessed Pharaoh again and then left his presence. He gave the king honor and goodwill on his way out.
entries.47:11: Joseph settled his father and brothers in the best part of Egypt, the region of Rameses, just as Pharaoh had ordered. He provided them a real home.
entries.47:12: Joseph made sure his father, brothers, and all their households had enough food for their families. He took practical care of his relatives during the famine.
entries.47:13: The famine was so severe that there was no food anywhere, and both Egypt and Canaan were suffering badly. Everyone was affected, not just the poor.
entries.47:14: People spent all their money buying grain, and Joseph collected it all for Pharaoh's treasury. The famine drained the savings of ordinary people.
entries.47:15: When the people's money ran out, they begged Joseph for food and asked if he would let them die. They had nothing left to pay with.
entries.47:16: Joseph offered to trade grain for their livestock since their money was gone. He was finding a way to keep them fed without giving food away for nothing.
entries.47:17: The people brought their horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys, and Joseph fed them for a year in exchange for the animals. They survived by trading what they owned.
entries.47:18: The next year the people admitted their money and livestock were all gone, and they had nothing left to offer but themselves and their land. They were completely out of options.
entries.47:19: The people asked Joseph to buy them and their land in exchange for food and seed, promising to serve Pharaoh. They were willing to give up their freedom to survive.
entries.47:20: Joseph acquired all the land in Egypt for Pharaoh because everyone sold it to buy food during the famine. The crisis transferred most of Egypt's land to the king.
entries.47:21: Joseph moved the people into towns across Egypt, making them servants of Pharaoh. The famine changed their whole way of life.
entries.47:22: Joseph did not take the priests' land, because Pharaoh gave them a regular food allowance and they didn't need to sell. They were treated differently from everyone else.
entries.47:23: Joseph told the people he had bought them and their land for Pharaoh, and he gave them seed to plant their fields. He gave them a way to start producing food again.
entries.47:24: Joseph set the rule that when harvest came, they would give one fifth to Pharaoh and keep four fifths for seed, food, and their families. It was a fair share that let them live.
entries.47:25: The people thanked Joseph for saving their lives and agreed to serve Pharaoh. They were grateful rather than resentful.
entries.47:26: Joseph made it a permanent law in Egypt that Pharaoh received a fifth of the harvest, except on priests' land. This arrangement shaped Egypt's economy for generations.
entries.47:27: Israel's family lived in Goshen, gained property there, and grew greatly in numbers and wealth. God was blessing them even in a foreign land.
entries.47:28: Jacob lived in Goshen for seventeen more years, reaching the age of 147. He had a long final season of life with his family.
entries.47:29: When Jacob knew he was near death, he made Joseph swear a solemn oath not to bury him in Egypt. He wanted assurance about where his body would rest.
entries.47:30: Jacob asked Joseph to carry his body back to Canaan and bury him with his ancestors, and Joseph promised to do it. Jacob wanted to be buried in the land God had promised his family.
entries.47:31: Jacob asked Joseph to swear the oath, Joseph did, and Jacob worshiped God from his bed. Even at the end of his life, Jacob turned to God in gratitude and faith.
entries.48:1: Joseph hears that his father Jacob is sick, so he takes his two sons to visit him. It reminds us to bring our families to be near loved ones in their final days.
entries.48:2: When Jacob learns Joseph has come, he gathers his strength and sits up in bed to receive him. Even weak and old, he makes an effort for an important moment with his son.
entries.48:3: Jacob reminds Joseph that God appeared to him years earlier at Luz and blessed him. He is passing on the story of God's faithfulness to the next generation.
entries.48:4: God promised Jacob a large family and the land of Canaan as an everlasting inheritance. Jacob recalls this promise because it shapes what he is about to do for Joseph's sons.
entries.48:5: Jacob adopts Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own, giving them equal standing with his other sons. This means they will share in the family inheritance just like Jacob's own children.
entries.48:6: Any further children Joseph has will still belong to him, but they will be counted under their brothers' names for the inheritance. The family line and property stay with the adopted sons.
entries.48:7: Jacob recalls how Rachel, Joseph's mother, died on the journey near Bethlehem and was buried there. He mentions this painful memory as he speaks about the sons she never got to raise.
entries.48:8: Jacob, whose eyesight is failing, asks who the two young men are. It shows he needs help identifying his own grandsons.
entries.48:9: Joseph explains they are his sons, given to him by God in Egypt, and Jacob asks to bless them. Joseph credits God for his children and welcomes his father's blessing on them.
entries.48:10: Jacob is old and cannot see well, so he draws the boys close and kisses and hugs them. Even with failing eyes, he shows them real affection.
entries.48:11: Jacob tells Joseph he never expected to see him again, yet God has let him see both Joseph and his children. It is a moment of gratitude for unexpected mercy.
entries.48:12: Joseph lifts the boys from his father's lap and bows low before him. He shows respect to his aging father as the blessing is about to be given.
entries.48:13: Joseph positions the boys so that Manasseh, the older, is at Jacob's right hand and Ephraim, the younger, at his left. He arranges them according to the usual custom for blessing.
entries.48:14: Jacob deliberately crosses his hands, putting his right hand on the younger Ephraim and his left on the older Manasseh. He is intentionally reversing the expected order.
entries.48:15: Jacob blesses Joseph by calling on the God his ancestors worshiped and who has cared for him his whole life. He names God as the one who has been faithful through everything.
entries.48:16: Jacob asks the angel who rescued him from harm to bless the boys and to let them carry on the family name and become a great people. He wants God's protection and promise to continue through them.
entries.48:17: Joseph is upset when he sees his father's right hand on Ephraim, the younger son, and tries to move it. He assumes his father has made a mistake.
entries.48:18: Joseph tells his father that the older son should get the right hand instead. He is trying to correct what looks like an error.
entries.48:19: Jacob refuses to change it, saying he knows what he is doing and that the younger will actually become greater than the older. God's choice does not always follow human expectations.
entries.48:20: Jacob blesses the boys that day, and people will later use their names when wishing blessings on others, with Ephraim placed ahead of Manasseh. Their names become a lasting picture of God's blessing.
entries.48:21: Jacob tells Joseph he is near death but that God will be with him and bring him back to the land of his ancestors. Even facing death, he trusts God's promise for the future.
entries.48:22: Jacob gives Joseph an extra share of land, the area of Shechem, which he says he took from the Amorites by force. Joseph receives a double portion compared to his brothers.
entries.49:1: Jacob calls his sons together to tell them what will happen to them in the future. It shows a father passing on important words to his family before he dies.
entries.49:2: Jacob asks his sons to come close and listen carefully to him. He wants their full attention for what he is about to say.
entries.49:3: Reuben is the firstborn, the son who should have received the greatest honor and strength. Being first gave him a special place in the family.
entries.49:4: Reuben lost his first place because he slept with his father's wife, which was a serious wrong. His actions cost him the honor he would have had.
entries.49:5: Simeon and Levi are described as brothers who use tricks and violence. Their weapons are tools of cruelty, not justice.
entries.49:6: Jacob refuses to join in their plans or meetings because of the violence they committed. He does not want to share in their guilt for killing people and harming animals.
entries.49:7: Their anger was fierce and cruel, so Jacob declares their anger is cursed. As a result, their descendants will be scattered among the other tribes of Israel.
entries.49:8: Judah will be praised by his brothers and will defeat his enemies. His brothers will bow down before him, showing his leadership.
entries.49:9: Judah is compared to a young lion that grows strong and rests securely. No one will dare to disturb him.
entries.49:10: Judah will keep the position of ruler, and a lawgiver will come from him until the rightful one arrives. The peoples will obey that ruler.
entries.49:11: This pictures great abundance, where even the vines are used to tie up a donkey and wine is so plentiful it is used for washing clothes. It shows the richness of Judah's future.
entries.49:12: His eyes will be dark from drinking wine and his teeth white from drinking milk. This is a picture of plenty and prosperity.
entries.49:13: Zebulun will live near the sea and become a harbor for ships. His land will reach toward Sidon.
entries.49:14: Issachar is compared to a strong donkey lying down among the sheep pens. It suggests strength combined with a settled, restful life.
entries.49:15: Issachar saw that rest was good and the land was pleasant, so he accepted hard work and became a servant. He chose comfort over freedom.
entries.49:16: Dan will judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel. His name sounds like the word for judge, and he will have a role in leading.
entries.49:17: Dan is compared to a snake beside the road that bites a horse's foot and makes the rider fall. This suggests cunning and the ability to trip up enemies.
entries.49:18: Jacob pauses to express his trust in God for rescue and deliverance. It is a personal prayer of hope in the middle of his predictions.
entries.49:19: Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will fight back and pursue them. He will not be defeated but will turn the attack around.
entries.49:20: Asher will have rich food and will provide delicacies fit for kings. His land will produce abundance.
entries.49:21: Naphtali is compared to a deer set free that gives birth to beautiful young. This suggests freedom and fruitfulness.
entries.49:22: Joseph is compared to a young ox or vine planted by a spring, suggesting strength and growth. He will be fruitful even in difficult conditions.
entries.49:23: Joseph was attacked by archers who shot at him and caused him pain. This refers to the hostility and suffering he faced.
entries.49:24: But his bow stayed strong because the mighty God of Jacob helped him. God is called the Stone of Israel, a firm foundation who protected Joseph.
entries.49:25: The God of his father will help Joseph and give him blessings from heaven above and from the deep below. These include blessings of family and fertility.
entries.49:26: Jacob asks that blessings greater than the ancient mountains come on Joseph's head. Joseph is honored because he was set apart from his brothers.
entries.49:27: Benjamin is compared to a wolf that hunts for prey in the morning and divides what it catches in the evening. This suggests fierceness and strength in battle.
entries.49:28: These are the twelve tribes of Israel, and Jacob gave each son a blessing suited to him. Each one received words about his future.
entries.49:29: Jacob tells his sons where to bury him, in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite. He wants to be laid to rest with his ancestors.
entries.49:30: The burial place is the cave in the field of Machpelah near Mamre in Canaan, which Abraham bought from Ephron. It was a family burial site.
entries.49:31: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah are all buried there. Jacob wants to join his family in that same place.
entries.49:32: The cave and field were bought for a price from the Hittites. This confirms that the burial place legally belonged to the family.
entries.49:33: After giving his final words, Jacob lay back on his bed and died, joining his ancestors. His long life ended peacefully after blessing his sons.
entries.50:1: Joseph was so sad about his father's death that he cried and kissed him. It shows that even strong leaders feel deep grief when they lose someone they love.
entries.50:2: Joseph told his skilled servants to prepare his father's body for burial with spices and linen. This was the normal way people honored a dead loved one in that culture.
entries.50:3: Preparing the body took forty days, and the Egyptians mourned for Jacob for seventy days. The long mourning shows how greatly Jacob was respected.
entries.50:4: After the mourning period, Joseph asked Pharaoh's officials to speak to Pharaoh for him. He needed permission to leave Egypt for the burial.
entries.50:5: Joseph explained that he had promised his father to bury him in Canaan, in a grave Jacob had prepared. He asked to go and do this, promising to return.
entries.50:6: Pharaoh agreed and told Joseph to go bury his father as he had promised. He honored the oath Joseph had made.
entries.50:7: Joseph traveled to Canaan for the burial, and many of Pharaoh's officials and Egypt's leaders went with him. This showed great respect for Joseph and his father.
entries.50:8: Joseph's whole family went too, except the young children and the animals, which stayed behind in Goshen. The family stayed together in their grief.
entries.50:9: Chariots and horsemen went along with the group, making it a large procession. The size of the group showed how important this burial was.
entries.50:10: When they reached a place near the Jordan, they held a great and bitter time of mourning for seven days. Their sorrow was open and deep.
entries.50:11: The local Canaanites saw how much the Egyptians were grieving and named the place after it. Even outsiders noticed the depth of their sorrow.
entries.50:12: Jacob's sons did exactly what their father had told them to do. They honored his final wishes.
entries.50:13: They carried Jacob's body to Canaan and buried him in the cave in the field Abraham had bought. This kept the family connected to the land God had promised them.
entries.50:14: After the burial, Joseph, his brothers, and everyone who had gone with them returned to Egypt. Life went on after the mourning.
entries.50:15: After their father died, Joseph's brothers became afraid that Joseph would finally punish them for what they had done to him. Guilt and fear came back once their father was gone.
entries.50:16: The brothers sent a message to Joseph, claiming their father had left instructions before he died. They were trying to find protection through their father's memory.
entries.50:17: They asked Joseph to forgive the wrong they had done to him, and Joseph cried when he heard it. Their plea moved him deeply.
entries.50:18: The brothers came and bowed down before Joseph, offering themselves as his servants. They were showing complete surrender out of fear.
entries.50:19: Joseph told them not to be afraid and asked whether he had any right to act as God. He knew punishment belonged to God, not to him.
entries.50:20: Joseph said they meant to harm him, but God turned it into something good that saved many people. God can bring good results even out of evil actions.
entries.50:21: Joseph told them not to fear and promised to care for them and their children, speaking kindly to them. He chose forgiveness and kindness over revenge.
entries.50:22: Joseph and his father's family continued living in Egypt, and Joseph lived to be a hundred and ten years old. His long life was seen as a sign of blessing.
entries.50:23: Joseph lived long enough to see his great-grandchildren and even held his grandson's children on his knees. He enjoyed the blessing of a large family.
entries.50:24: Before he died, Joseph told his brothers that God would remember them and lead them out of Egypt to the land he promised. He trusted God's promise even though it had not happened yet.
entries.50:25: Joseph made the Israelites promise to carry his bones with them when God rescued them from Egypt. He wanted to be buried in the promised land and showed faith in God's future rescue.
entries.50:26: Joseph died at a hundred and ten, and his body was prepared and placed in a coffin in Egypt. His body stayed in Egypt, waiting for the day God would keep his promise.
